extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, merchants, and readers of political economy (legislators, economists, and informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical standards for structuring corn (grain) laws, import/export duties, bounties, carrying trade, and treaties of commerce — aimed at evaluating trade policy effects on home supply, tillage, and national advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of inland trade for home supply and tillage
rubrics_metrics.description: The inland corn trade has derived all the liberty and protection it has enjoyed from statute and 'both the supply of the home market and the interest of tillage are much more effectually promoted by the inland, than either by the importation or exportation trade.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inland trade is the nearest, most convenient, and most important market for corn; laws that secure and liberate the inland trade (e.g., 15th Charles II c.7) encourage tillage and plentiful home supply. Policy should prioritize protecting and enabling inland dealers over measures focused on foreign trade when the goal is to secure domestic supply and cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importation contributes to immediate home supply and real wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade of the merchant-importer of foreign corn for home consumption 'evidently contributes to the immediate supply of the home market' and, though it lowers the money price of corn, does not diminish its real value or the quantity of labour it can maintain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free importation enlarges the home market and can increase real wages by lowering nominal prices and raising the real value of silver. Farmers' nominal receipts may fall but their real wealth and incentives to cultivate need not be harmed if importation is not unduly restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on importation are improper as general policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of temporary statutes allowing importation in scarcity 'sufficiently demonstrates the impropriety of this general one' (i.e., general restraints on importation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High duties that functionally prohibit imports are harmful; resorting routinely to temporary suspensions of prohibitions in scarcity shows the base policy is flawed. Import restraints should not be the default; if used at all they must be exceptional and temporary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of exportation encourages cultivation and surplus production
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition of exportation 'limits the improvement and cultivation of the country' while freedom of exportation 'enables it to extend cultivation for the supply of foreign nations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing exportation permits producers to seek foreign markets for surplus, incentivizing higher production. Export prohibition will keep production only at bare domestic-consumption levels and thus generally reduce improvements in cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export prohibition (if ever used) must be at very high prices
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The price at which exportation of corn is prohibited, if it is ever to be prohibited, ought always to be a very high price.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If export bans are imposed to protect domestic supply, the threshold should be set very high to avoid unnecessary suppression of merchants' access to markets and to avoid perverting the ordinary laws of justice for tenuous 'reasons of state.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties on exportation are improper and should be reduced or abolished
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounties (payments for export) were enacted 'in order to force' exportation and tend to raise home prices, creating dearth; 'If bounties are as improper as I have endeavoured to prove them to be, the sooner they cease, and the lower they are, so much the better.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bounties distort incentives, encouraging exports at times injurious to home supply and wasting public revenue. Policy should minimize bounties and withdraw them at lower prices (or abolish them altogether). Avoid designs where bounty withdrawal coincides awkwardly with export prohibition thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incoherent thresholds where bounty withdrawal and export prohibition coincide
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper 'in prohibiting exportation altogether at those precise prices at which that bounty, which was given in order to force it, is withdrawn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation should not create perverse incentives by withdrawing bounties at the same price where export is then prohibited; either withdraw bounties earlier or allow export at higher prices to avoid contradictory policy signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carrying trade and bonded warehousing (re-import for re-export) support home supply
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade of the merchant-carrier (import to export again) 'contributes to the plentiful supply of the home market' because carriers will often sell in the home market at lower prices to avoid reloading, freight, and insurance costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting carrying trade and bonded warehouses (import lodged in warehouse under joint locks to be re-exported duty-free) in principal ports is beneficial; duties and regulations that effectively prohibit the carrying trade reduce domestic supply and increase prices. Expand practical access to such warehousing where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: High duties that amount to prohibition are harmful and produce temporary remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: High duties on importation worked 'in effect prohibited' imports and were repeatedly suspended by temporary statutes in scarcity — demonstrating the impropriety of the permanent restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When duties are set so high as to prohibit normal trade, governments will be forced to enact ad-hoc exceptions in crises. Sound policy avoids permanently prohibitive duties and relies on stable, predictable regimes that do not require frequent emergency corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation should not prevent farmers selling to the best market (justice over state reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: To hinder the farmer from sending his goods 'at all times to the best market, is evidently to sacrifice the ordinary laws of justice to an idea of public utility... which ought to be exercised only ... in cases of the most urgent necessity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade restrictions that deny individuals their right to dispose of produce to the best market violate ordinary justice and should be justified only by extreme necessity. Default policy should respect market choice and private property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export restraints may be justifiable in very small states but rarely in great countries
rubrics_metrics.description: In small states (e.g., a Swiss canton or little Italian states) it 'may, perhaps, sometimes be necessary to restrain the exportation of corn' but 'in such great countries as France or England, it scarce ever can.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy must be sensitive to scale and communication: large integrated countries with ample internal and external markets need fewer export restrictions; small, poorly connected states may occasionally require protection but exceptions should be narrowly tailored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties granting exclusive commercial favours create foreign monopolies and reduce national exchangeable value
rubrics_metrics.description: When a nation permits entry or exempts duties for one foreign country it grants 'a sort of monopoly' to the favoured nation's merchants; this makes goods of that foreign nation more expensive for domestic consumers and lowers the exchangeable value of the favouring country's produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferential treaties that favour foreign producers advantage those foreign merchants and disadvantage domestic merchants and manufacturers. Such treaties may lessen the gain that would be obtained under free competition and must be weighed against any compensating benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiving specie via treaty is not as advantageous as direct foreign trade of consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaties supposed advantageous because they bring a balance in gold and silver (e.g., Methuen treaty) are inferior to direct foreign trade of consumption: 'A direct foreign trade of consumption is always more advantageous than a round-about one' purchased via specie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should prefer direct trade in consumables to arrangements aiming primarily to secure specie inflows. Relying on specie as an intermediate to obtain goods is less efficient and may employ unnecessarily large capital compared to direct trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obsession with balance of trade (specific country balances) is misleading policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The more gold imported from one country, the less must be imported from others; apparent favourable balances with some countries imply unfavourable balances with others — the balance-of-trade fixation is 'silly' and misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid policy based on achieving favourable bilateral balances with particular nations; focus instead on the overall efficiency and gain from trade. National advantage is not secured by privileging one bilateral balance at the cost of general economic efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security of property and freedom of industry matter more than particular restrictive regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosperity of Great Britain can be accounted for largely by 'that security which the laws in Great Britain give to every man, that he shall enjoy the fruits of his own labour' rather than by specific restrictive laws like bounties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional guarantees (security of property, liberty to pursue industry) are the primary drivers of national improvement and should take precedence over fine-tuned mercantile regulations. Good general institutions can overcome many ill-advised commercial restrictions.
